subtopic_detail: worsening hand shake in a man whose mood medication was increased three months before the tremor began
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 61-year-old man with a worsening hand tremor. He has spilled his tea twice this week and is embarrassed signing documents at the bank. He tells you the shaking started about six months ago and has become steadily more noticeable.

He has bipolar disorder that has been stable for years, and his sodium valproate was increased from 1000 mg to 1500 mg daily nine months ago after a brief hypomanic episode. He also takes perindopril. He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and says alcohol makes no difference to the shaking. There is no family history of tremor. On examination there is a symmetrical fine tremor of both outstretched hands that is present throughout finger to nose movement and absent at rest. There is no rigidity, no bradykinesia on rapid alternating movements, no reduction in arm swing and no facial masking. Gait is normal, and there is no head tremor or vocal tremor. Thyroid function and a serum valproate level are within their reference ranges.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical fine postural and action tremor of both hands, absent at rest, no head or vocal tremor
data_table.Parkinsonian features: No rigidity, no bradykinesia on rapid alternating movements, preserved arm swing, no facial masking, normal gait
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, serum valproate concentration within the therapeutic range
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1500 mg daily increased from 1000 mg nine months ago, perindopril

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request serum caeruloplasmin with a twenty four hour urinary copper and a slit lamp examination
options.rationale: Wilson disease must be excluded in any movement disorder presenting under the age of forty, and it can cause tremor alongside psychiatric symptoms. First presentation at sixty one with a clear temporal relationship to a dose increase makes it very unlikely. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Wilson disease)

options.text: Commence primidone at a low dose at night and increase it gradually over the following month
options.rationale: Primidone is the other established treatment for essential tremor and is effective, so this shares the reasoning error rather than the pharmacology. It adds a second sedating anticonvulsant to a patient already taking one, when the simpler answer is to address the causative dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence propranolol for essential tremor and titrate the dose according to his response
options.rationale: Propranolol is first line for essential tremor and would help the tremor symptomatically whatever its cause, which makes it tempting. Essential tremor is usually longstanding with a family history and characteristic alcohol responsiveness, and adding a drug to treat another drug's adverse effect is poor practice when the dose can be reduced. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Discuss a reduction of the valproate dose with his treating psychiatrist and review in six weeks
options.rationale: A symmetrical postural and action tremor beginning after a valproate dose increase, with no parkinsonian signs and no alcohol responsiveness, is drug induced. Valproate tremor is dose related and occurs at therapeutic concentrations, so dose reduction in partnership with the prescriber is the first step. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for dopamine transporter imaging to assess for a nigrostriatal degenerative process
options.rationale: Functional dopaminergic imaging is used when a parkinsonian syndrome is suspected but the clinical picture is equivocal. A purely postural and action tremor with no rest component, rigidity or bradykinesia gives no clinical basis for the referral. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Drug induced tremor is among the commonest causes of tremor in adults and is routinely misattributed to essential tremor or to early Parkinson disease. It is characteristically symmetrical, postural and action predominant, and temporally related to starting a drug or increasing a dose. Sodium valproate causes tremor in up to a quarter of patients, it is dose related, and it occurs at therapeutic serum concentrations, so a normal level does not exclude it. Other frequent culprits are lithium, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, beta agonists, corticosteroids, amiodarone, thyroxine and caffeine, while dopamine antagonists including antipsychotics and metoclopramide instead produce a rest tremor with other parkinsonian features. The correct first response to a drug induced tremor is to review the offending medication, ideally with the prescriber where the drug is treating a serious condition, rather than to add a second medication to suppress the symptom.
key_points: Drug induced tremor is symmetrical, postural and action predominant, and dose related.
Valproate tremor occurs at therapeutic levels, so a normal concentration excludes nothing.
Dopamine antagonists cause a rest tremor with other parkinsonian features instead.
Essential tremor suggests itself through duration, family history and alcohol responsiveness.
Review the causative drug before adding a second drug to suppress the symptom.
explanation.pearls: Never reduce or stop a mood stabiliser unilaterally in a patient with bipolar disorder, because relapse risk after abrupt withdrawal is substantial, particularly with lithium where rapid cessation can precipitate mania within weeks; the change is negotiated with the treating psychiatrist.

subtopic_detail: widespread scaly oval trunk rash also involving both palms and soles in a young man
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old man with a rash that appeared ten days ago and has spread across his trunk. He is not particularly itchy. He had a mild sore throat and felt tired for a few days beforehand.

He assumed it was a viral rash and has been using a moisturiser. He is otherwise well with no fever now. On examination there are multiple oval salmon pink scaly macules and papules 5 to 15 mm across scattered over the trunk, with the long axis of the lesions following the skin lines over the back. There are similar scaly copper coloured papules on both palms and both soles, and a few on the shaft of the penis. There is no single larger patch preceding the eruption that he can recall. He has non tender rubbery lymph nodes palpable in both axillae and both groins, and there are a few small moth eaten patches of hair loss on the occipital scalp. He has had four male sexual partners in the past year and last tested for sexually transmitted infections two years ago.

data_table.Examination: Oval salmon pink scaly papules over the trunk following skin lines, scaly copper coloured papules on both palms and soles, papules on the penile shaft
data_table.Lymph nodes: Non tender rubbery generalised lymphadenopathy in both axillae and both groins
data_table.Scalp: Patchy moth eaten hair loss over the occipital scalp
data_table.History: Four male sexual partners in the preceding year, last sexually transmitted infection screening two years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a monospot test with a full blood examination and liver function tests this week
options.rationale: Infectious mononucleosis causes a prodrome, lymphadenopathy and occasionally a rash, particularly after aminopenicillin exposure, so it is a fair differential for the systemic features. It does not produce palmoplantar scaly papules or moth eaten alopecia. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Infectious mononucleosis)

options.text: Request syphilis serology together with a full sexually transmitted infection screen today
options.rationale: Palmoplantar involvement, generalised non tender lymphadenopathy, moth eaten alopecia and mucosal lesions after a flu like prodrome are secondary syphilis, which mimics several common eruptions. Serology confirms it and the full screen is required because of the high rate of coinfection. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Take skin scrapings for fungal microscopy and culture and start topical terbinafine cream
options.rationale: Scrapings investigate tinea corporis, which produces annular lesions with a raised scaly leading edge and central clearing rather than uniformly scaly oval papules. Widespread simultaneous onset with systemic features is not a dermatophyte pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Reassure him that this is a self limiting eruption and review him again in six to eight weeks
options.rationale: Pityriasis rosea is the near pair and does produce oval scaly lesions following skin lines after a viral prodrome, so the trunk appearance alone genuinely fits. It spares the palms and soles and does not cause generalised lymphadenopathy or patchy alopecia, and watchful waiting would leave syphilis untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Prescribe a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment with an emollient twice daily
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid suits guttate psoriasis or an eczematous eruption, which do not involve the penile shaft in this pattern or produce rubbery generalised lymphadenopathy. Suppressing the rash would also obscure the presentation without treating the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Secondary syphilis appears weeks to a few months after the primary chancre and is the great imitator of dermatology, being mistaken for pityriasis rosea, guttate psoriasis, viral exanthem and drug eruption. The findings that should redirect thinking are involvement of the palms and soles, which almost no other papulosquamous eruption shares, generalised non tender rubbery lymphadenopathy, moth eaten patchy alopecia, mucous patches and condylomata lata. Diagnosis rests on serology, with a treponemal test used for screening and a non treponemal titre such as the rapid plasma reagin used to assess activity and to monitor the response to treatment. Treatment of early syphilis is a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin, and patients should be warned about the Jarisch Herxheimer reaction in the first 24 hours. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus and other sexually transmitted infections, and partner notification, are integral to management.
key_points: Palmoplantar scaly papules in a widespread eruption should prompt syphilis serology.
Generalised non tender lymphadenopathy and moth eaten alopecia support the diagnosis.
Pityriasis rosea follows skin lines but spares palms and soles and lacks systemic signs.
Treponemal serology screens; a non treponemal titre monitors treatment response.
Early syphilis is treated with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin.
explanation.pearls: Warn every patient treated for early syphilis about the Jarisch Herxheimer reaction, a self limiting fever, rigors and headache within 24 hours of the first penicillin dose, because it is commonly mistaken for penicillin allergy and leads to unnecessary avoidance of the only recommended treatment.

subtopic_detail: night time hand tingling with flattening of the muscle bulk at the base of the thumb
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 57-year-old cleaner with eighteen months of tingling in her right hand that wakes her most nights and is relieved by shaking the hand over the side of the bed. She has recently started dropping cups and cannot reliably do up buttons or turn a key.

She was given a wrist splint by a physiotherapist a year ago and wore it nightly for three months with some early benefit that has since been lost. She has no neck pain and no pain radiating from the neck. She has no diabetes and thyroid function tested last month was normal. On examination there is visible flattening of the muscle bulk over the ball of the thumb on the right compared with the left, and thumb abduction against resistance is weak on the right. Sensation is reduced to light touch over the palmar surfaces of the thumb, index and middle fingers, with normal sensation over the little finger and over the skin at the base of the thumb. Neck movements are full and painless, and reflexes in both arms are normal and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Visible right thenar wasting with weak thumb abduction against resistance, normal bulk on the left
data_table.Sensory findings: Reduced light touch over the palmar thumb, index and middle fingers, spared little finger and spared thenar eminence skin
data_table.Cervical spine: Full painless neck movements, no radicular pain, normal and symmetrical upper limb reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, no diabetes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Inject the carpal tunnel with corticosteroid and review her symptoms again in six weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroid injection produces useful short term relief in moderate disease and is a legitimate step before surgery in patients without weakness. Its effect wanes over months and it does not address structural compression that has already caused axonal loss. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence pregabalin for neuropathic pain and refer her for hand therapy and nerve gliding exercises
options.rationale: Neuropathic agents and hand therapy address symptoms and may improve comfort, and nerve gliding has modest supporting evidence. Neither reverses compression, and treating symptomatically while the thenar muscles waste risks a permanent functional deficit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refit a neutral position night wrist splint and arrange a review of her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Nocturnal neutral splinting is the correct first line for mild to moderate carpal tunnel syndrome without motor signs and often works well. Once there is thenar wasting, splinting will not restore lost motor axons and delays a decompression that becomes less effective the longer it waits. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine to assess for nerve root compression
options.rationale: Cervical imaging targets a C6 radiculopathy, the near pair, which gives neck pain, a dermatomal sensory pattern extending above the wrist, and an altered biceps or brachioradialis reflex. Painless full neck movement with normal reflexes and sensory loss confined to the hand argues against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies and surgical assessment for decompression of the nerve
options.rationale: Thenar wasting with weak thumb abduction indicates established motor axonal loss, which does not recover with conservative treatment and can progress to permanent weakness. Surgical release with prior electrophysiological confirmation is indicated rather than further conservative measures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and results from compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum. The classic history is nocturnal paraesthesia in the median distribution relieved by shaking the hand, and symptoms are often reported across the whole hand even though the sensory deficit spares the little finger. A useful anatomical clue is that the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve proximal to the tunnel, so sensation over the thenar eminence skin is preserved, which distinguishes the entrapment from a more proximal median lesion or a C6 radiculopathy. Management is stratified by severity: nocturnal neutral wrist splinting with activity modification for mild to moderate disease, corticosteroid injection as a temporising measure, and surgical decompression for severe disease. The findings that define severe disease and mandate surgical referral are thenar wasting, weakness of thumb abduction, constant rather than intermittent sensory loss, and failure of conservative treatment.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesia relieved by shaking the hand is the characteristic history.
Preserved sensation over the thenar eminence skin reflects the spared palmar cutaneous branch.
Thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction define severe disease requiring surgery.
Splinting and injection are for mild to moderate disease without motor signs.
Sensory recovery after decompression is reliable, but motor recovery is slow and incomplete.
explanation.pearls: Test thumb abduction by asking the patient to raise the thumb vertically out of the plane of the palm against your resistance, because this isolates abductor pollicis brevis, the one thenar muscle supplied solely by the median nerve, and its weakness is what converts a conservative management plan into a surgical referral.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

subtopic_detail: painful stiff shoulder in a woman whose passive external rotation is as restricted as her active movement
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 53-year-old woman with six months of right shoulder pain. It began without injury, was worst at night for the first three months and woke her whenever she rolled onto that side, and the night pain has now eased while the stiffness has become the dominant problem.

She can no longer reach behind her back to fasten a bra or reach up to a high cupboard. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and her most recent glycated haemoglobin was 8.4 per cent (target under 7.0). On examination active abduction is limited to 80 degrees and active external rotation to 10 degrees. When you relax her arm and move it passively, external rotation remains restricted at 10 degrees with a firm end point and reproduces her pain. There is no tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint and no painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees. Power in the rotator cuff muscles is preserved within the available range, and a radiograph of the shoulder shows no calcification, no fracture and preserved joint space.

data_table.Examination: Active abduction limited to 80 degrees and active external rotation to 10 degrees
data_table.Passive movement: Passive external rotation equally restricted at 10 degrees with a firm end point, reproducing the pain
data_table.Other findings: No acromioclavicular tenderness, no painful arc, rotator cuff power preserved within the available range
data_table.Investigations: Shoulder radiograph showing no calcification, fracture or joint space loss, glycated haemoglobin 8.4 per cent (target under 7.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer a subacromial corticosteroid injection with a graded rotator cuff strengthening programme
options.rationale: Subacromial injection and cuff strengthening treat subacromial pain syndrome, the near pair, in which passive range is preserved even when active movement is painful and limited. Injecting the subacromial space does not reach an inflamed and contracted glenohumeral capsule. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Offer an intra articular corticosteroid injection with supervised physiotherapy and glycaemic review
options.rationale: Equal restriction of active and passive external rotation with a normal radiograph is adhesive capsulitis, and intra articular corticosteroid with physiotherapy gives the greatest benefit during the painful and stiffening phases. Optimising glycaemic control matters because diabetes both predisposes to the condition and prolongs it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Refer for urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulder to assess for a rotator cuff tear
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is appropriate for suspected cuff tear with weakness out of proportion to pain, or when surgery is being considered. A full thickness tear reduces active movement while passive range stays free, and imaging is not needed to make this diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Advise rest from overhead activity with regular analgesia and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Analgesia is part of care but immobilisation accelerates capsular contracture and worsens the stiffness that is now her main complaint. Three months of waiting during the stiffening phase loses the window in which injection is most useful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Refer for arthroscopic capsular release and manipulation of the shoulder under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Capsular release is genuinely effective and is the escalation for disabling stiffness persisting beyond six to twelve months despite conservative treatment. Offering it at six months before injection and physiotherapy have been tried is premature for a condition that usually resolves. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Frozen shoulder)

explanation.summary: Adhesive capsulitis is a fibro inflammatory contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule that classically evolves through a painful freezing phase of two to nine months, a stiff frozen phase of four to twelve months, and a thawing phase over one to three years. The defining physical sign is loss of passive as well as active movement, with external rotation affected earliest and most severely, and a firm capsular end feel rather than pain limited guarding. That single finding separates it from the rotator cuff disorders, in which passive range is preserved, and a normal radiograph excludes glenohumeral osteoarthritis, which gives a similar pattern with joint space loss. Diabetes is the strongest risk factor, increasing incidence roughly fivefold and predicting a longer and more refractory course, and thyroid disease, Dupuytren disease and previous shoulder immobilisation are also associated. Intra articular corticosteroid combined with supervised physiotherapy gives the best short and medium term outcomes, particularly when given early, and hydrodilatation, capsular release or manipulation under anaesthesia are reserved for disabling stiffness persisting beyond six to twelve months.
key_points: Equal restriction of active and passive movement with a firm end feel is the defining sign.
External rotation is affected earliest and most severely.
Rotator cuff disorders preserve passive range; osteoarthritis shows joint space loss.
Diabetes raises incidence roughly fivefold and predicts a more refractory course.
Intra articular corticosteroid with physiotherapy is most effective when given early.
explanation.pearls: Stabilise the scapula with one hand while testing external rotation with the elbow at the side, because scapulothoracic substitution otherwise masks up to 30 degrees of lost glenohumeral rotation and makes a frozen shoulder look like a cuff problem.

subtopic_detail: continuous spinning for eighteen hours with a normal head impulse test and a normal early brain scan
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 63-year-old man who woke yesterday evening with the room spinning and has been continuously dizzy since, unable to stand without help and vomiting repeatedly. He has hypertension and smokes fifteen cigarettes a day.

He has had no hearing loss, no tinnitus and no headache, and he reports no double vision, no slurred speech and no limb weakness. On examination he is distressed and pale but alert and fully oriented. There is horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase to the left when he looks ahead, which reverses direction and beats to the right when he looks to the right. Horizontal head impulse testing produces no corrective saccade in either direction. Alternate cover testing shows a small vertical realignment of the right eye. Limb power, tone and reflexes are normal and there is no dysmetria on finger to nose testing, but he cannot sit unsupported on the trolley without falling to the left. A non contrast computed tomography scan of the brain performed an hour ago is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Eye movements: Horizontal nystagmus beating left in primary gaze that reverses to beat right on right gaze, small vertical realignment of the right eye on alternate cover testing
data_table.Head impulse test: No corrective saccade on rapid horizontal head impulse in either direction
data_table.Neurological: Normal limb power, tone and reflexes, no dysmetria on finger to nose testing, unable to sit unsupported without falling to the left
data_table.Imaging: Non contrast computed tomography of the brain reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform the Dix Hallpike manoeuvre and treat any positional nystagmus with particle repositioning
options.rationale: Positional testing is for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which produces brief paroxysms lasting under a minute on position change rather than eighteen hours of continuous spinning. Repositioning a patient with a posterior fossa infarct offers no benefit and delays imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Admit under the stroke service for magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion weighted sequences
options.rationale: A normal head impulse test, direction changing nystagmus and vertical ocular misalignment together indicate a central cause, and truncal ataxia out of proportion to limb findings supports it. Computed tomography misses most acute posterior fossa infarcts, so diffusion weighted magnetic resonance imaging is required. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Arrange outpatient audiometry and a carotid duplex ultrasound with review in the next week
options.rationale: Carotid imaging assesses the anterior circulation, whereas the vestibular system is supplied by the posterior circulation, so a normal duplex would be falsely reassuring. Discharging a man who cannot sit unsupported is unsafe regardless of the investigation chosen. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Give intravenous prochlorperazine, rehydrate him and reassess his symptoms in four hours
options.rationale: Antiemetic and fluid resuscitation are reasonable supportive measures alongside investigation and will make him more comfortable. Used as the management plan they suppress the vestibular signs that the examination depends on and lose time in a stroke pathway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence a tapering course of oral prednisolone and refer him for vestibular rehabilitation
options.rationale: This treats vestibular neuritis, which is the diagnosis the duration and the continuous vertigo would otherwise suggest. Neuritis gives an abnormal head impulse test with a corrective saccade towards the affected side and unidirectional nystagmus that does not change direction, and this man has neither. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Acute vestibular syndrome describes continuous vertigo lasting more than 24 hours with nystagmus, nausea and gait unsteadiness, and the clinical task is to separate vestibular neuritis from a posterior circulation stroke, which accounts for roughly a quarter of cases in patients with vascular risk factors. The three step bedside examination known by the acronym HINTS comprises the horizontal head impulse test, observation of nystagmus in different gaze positions, and a test of skew using alternate cover. Each component reads counterintuitively: a normal head impulse test is the worrying result, because a peripheral lesion produces a corrective saccade and an intact vestibulo ocular reflex means the periphery is working. Performed in the right patient this combination outperforms early magnetic resonance imaging for detecting stroke, and it vastly outperforms computed tomography, which misses the large majority of acute posterior fossa infarcts. The other high value bedside sign is severe truncal ataxia: inability to sit or stand unsupported is rare in neuritis and should be treated as central until proven otherwise.
key_points: A normal head impulse test in acute vestibular syndrome is a central finding, not a reassuring one.
Direction changing gaze evoked nystagmus and skew deviation both indicate a central lesion.
Computed tomography misses most acute posterior fossa infarcts and cannot exclude one.
Inability to sit or stand unsupported points strongly to a central cause.
HINTS applies only to continuous acute vestibular syndrome, never to episodic vertigo.
explanation.pearls: HINTS is valid only in a patient with continuous vertigo and nystagmus at the time of examination; applying it to someone whose episodic vertigo has already settled produces a falsely reassuring result, because a normal head impulse test in an asymptomatic patient means nothing at all.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of vertigo
